name: papers
title: Find duplicates, then sort your administrative papers
pitch: Two parts. First, find duplicate files in a folder of papers and move the extra copies aside. Then, read the text of each PDF and sort it into a theme folder (tax, bank, health…) and a year. Part 1 is medium, part 2 is hard.

steps.do: Part 1, duplicates. COPY a folder of papers (PDFs, scans, photos of documents) into a test folder, with at least one duplicate you made on purpose.
steps.done: the copy holds a few files, and one of them twice under two names.
steps.hint: `cp invoice.pdf invoice-copy.pdf` makes a duplicate you know about.
steps.why: A known duplicate is your test: if the program doesn't find it, the program is wrong.

steps.do: List the files of the folder with std::fs::read_dir.
steps.hint: read_dir returns a Result of an iterator of Results: each level can fail, so handle each one.
steps.why: Every file operation can fail (permissions, a file deleted meanwhile). Rust shows it in the types, so you can't forget.

steps.do: List the files of every subfolder too.
steps.done: files deep in subfolders are listed.
steps.hint: A recursive function, or the walkdir crate.
steps.why: A folder tree is a recursive structure: a folder holds files and folders. A recursive function follows its shape.

steps.do: Group the files by size in a HashMap. Only files with the same size can be duplicates.
steps.done: the program prints the groups with more than one file.
steps.why: Comparing sizes first is cheap and rules out most files. Doing the cheap check before the expensive one is how fast programs are built.

steps.do: Compute a hash of the files that share a size, and group them by hash.
steps.done: your duplicate is found, and two different files of the same size are not.
steps.hint: The sha2 crate; read the file and feed it to the hasher, then compare the results.
steps.why: A hash is a fingerprint of the content: same content, same hash. Two different files with the same SHA-256 is practically impossible.

steps.do: Print a report: each group of duplicates, and the space they waste.
steps.why: A number like "1.2 GB wasted" is what makes someone decide to clean up.

steps.do: Dry run: print which copies would be moved, keeping one of each.
steps.hint: Keep the first one of each group (the shortest path, for example) and list the others.
steps.why: Deciding which copy to keep is a rule you choose. Printing it first lets you check the rule before it acts.

steps.do: Move the extra copies into a duplicates/ folder. Never delete: the user decides.
steps.done: the folder holds one copy of each file, and the extras are in duplicates/.
steps.hint: `std::fs::rename` moves a file within the same disk.
steps.why: Moving instead of deleting makes every mistake reversible. Good tools leave the final decision to people.

steps.do: Part 2, sorting by theme. Extract the text of one PDF and print it.
steps.done: you see the words of the paper.
steps.hint: The pdf-extract crate has a function that takes a path and returns the text.
steps.why: Many PDFs hold real text inside; scans are pictures and hold none. You'll handle those later.

steps.do: Write a list of themes with their keywords (tax, bank, health, house, salary…) in a config file, and load it.
steps.done: the program prints each theme with its keywords.
steps.hint: TOML: `[themes]` with `tax = ["tax", "income", …]`, loaded into a HashMap<String, Vec<String>>.
steps.why: Keywords change from one country and one language to another. In a config file, anyone can adapt them without touching the code.

steps.do: Score each theme: how many of its keywords appear in the paper. Pick the theme with the best score.
steps.done: a tax paper gets the "tax" theme.
steps.hint: Lowercase the text first (`to_lowercase`), then count with `contains` or `matches`.
steps.why: Scoring is a simple form of classification, the same idea behind spam filters.

steps.do: Papers with no matching keyword, or no text at all, go to unknown.
steps.done: a random image goes to unknown.
steps.hint: A score of 0 means no theme.
steps.why: A program must say "I don't know" instead of guessing wrong. unknown is a pile you sort by hand.

steps.do: Dry run: print where each paper would go (`invoice.pdf -> house`).
steps.hint: Reuse the dry-run idea from part 1.
steps.why: Same safety, new rule: check the plan before acting.

steps.do: Copy the papers into their theme folders.
steps.done: each paper is in its theme folder.
steps.why: Copy first: the originals stay where they were until you trust the result.

steps.do: Find a date in the text and sort by year inside each theme.
steps.hint: The regex crate: a pattern for dd/mm/yyyy and yyyy-mm-dd.
steps.why: Regexes find patterns in text. Dates are written many ways, so expect to adjust your pattern after a few real papers.

steps.do: Handle two papers with the same name in the same folder: don't let one overwrite the other.
steps.hint: Check `exists()` before copying, and add a number to the name.
steps.why: Same lesson as every project that moves files: never overwrite silently.

steps.do: Optional: read scanned papers (pictures with no text) with OCR, using tesseract.
steps.done: a scanned paper gets a theme instead of unknown.
steps.hint: Run tesseract with `std::process::Command` and read its output.
steps.why: Calling another program from Rust lets you use decades of work (tesseract) in a few lines.
